h1: Large format porcelain tiling in Stoke Poges

hero.intro: Stoke Poges is a village of large plots and substantial houses, best known for Stoke Park's golf and country club, with housing ranging from older period detached homes to more recent executive-style builds set well back on sizeable gardens. That extra space tends to carry through into the bathrooms themselves — larger footprints mean fewer awkward corners and more continuous runs of floor, which is exactly where large format porcelain earns its keep. We work fit-only: you buy the tiles, sanitaryware, brassware and furniture, we strip out, first-fix, tile, plumb and snag, from £3,500.

sections.heading: Bigger rooms, fewer joins, more to get right
sections.body: One advantage of the larger Stoke Poges plots we see is that bathrooms are often generously sized rather than squeezed into a converted box room. A bigger floor area means we can lay large format slabs with fewer cuts and fewer joins across the room, which is where the material looks its best — a near-seamless plane rather than a patchwork of cut pieces. But a bigger continuous run also means the substrate has to be flat over a bigger area; there's more room for a long run to find a dip or a hump, so we check level across the whole floor plate before tiling starts, not just in a corner.

sections.heading: What generous plots mean for layout changes
sections.body: Because many Stoke Poges properties sit on sizeable gardens with room to manoeuvre, we often have more freedom to move a waste run, widen a doorway for level access, or add a second en-suite off a principal bedroom than a terraced house would allow. Where a layout changes — a bath moving to a different wall, a shower replacing a corner bath — the new floor area needs its own flatness check and its own adhesive bed; we don't assume the existing subfloor is suitable just because the room is large.

sections.heading: Full adhesive coverage and lippage control
sections.body: Large slabs need a full bed of adhesive across their entire underside, combed onto the substrate and back-buttered onto the tile, so there's no void that can crack under a standing load. We use levelling clips through the floor and wall tiling so neighbouring slab edges finish flush rather than catching the light differently — lippage is one of the most common complaints with large format tiling done without the right system, and it's avoidable with the right prep time.

sections.heading: Start with a survey
sections.body: We begin with a paid £125 survey to check the substrate, confirm the layout and talk through what the room will need before you order tiles. Call or WhatsApp 07399 651836 to book a survey for your Stoke Poges bathroom.

faqs.q: Does a bigger bathroom make large format tiling easier?
faqs.a: It can reduce the number of cuts and joins, which suits the material well, but a larger floor area also needs to be checked for flatness across its whole span — any dip over a longer run still has to be corrected before tiling.

faqs.q: Can you move the waste pipe to change my bathroom layout?
faqs.a: Often, yes — larger Stoke Poges properties generally give us more room to reroute a waste run or reposition a shower than a smaller or terraced property would allow, though it depends on what we find at survey.

faqs.q: Do I need an uneven subfloor fixed before you tile?
faqs.a: Yes, for large format porcelain it's essential. We'll level the substrate with self-levelling compound, additional ply, or both, depending on what the survey shows.

faqs.q: What's included in the fit-only price?
faqs.a: Strip-out, first-fix plumbing and electrics, tiling, final-fix plumbing and snagging. You buy the sanitaryware, brassware, tiles and furniture separately.

faqs.q: How long does a large format tiling job take in a bigger bathroom?
faqs.a: It varies with room size and layout changes, but we'll give you a realistic programme at survey stage once we've seen the space and confirmed what you're installing.
